headline: UConn parent asks court to halt Storrs blue-light phone removals
dek: A judge declined to issue an immediate shutdown order but set an Oct. 9 hearing on a parent’s request to keep the campus emergency phones operating while the dispute proceeds.
body: A parent of a University of Connecticut student is asking a state court to pause the university’s removal of blue-light emergency phones from the Storrs campus, opening a new legal fight over whether a physical emergency network can be retired as cellphones and safety apps become more common. The court declined to grant an immediate, before-hearing injunction, but scheduled a remote preliminary hearing for Oct. 9 at 9:30 a.m., according to reporting by [NBC Connecticut](https://www.nbcconnecticut.com/news/local/uconn-parent-sues-school-to-stop-removal-of-blue-light-emergency-phones/3780793/) and [Hearst Connecticut Media](https://www.newstimes.com/news/education/article/uconn-blue-emergency-phones-lawsuit-22457637.php).

Billyjoe Contreras filed the application Oct. 1 in Connecticut Superior Court, citing concerns about campus safety. His request would bar UConn from disconnecting, disabling, removing or decommissioning the existing blue-light phones and associated safety lights at Storrs while the case is pending. He also asks the university to continue maintaining and operating the system. The immediate request was an ex parte application, meaning Contreras sought temporary relief before a full hearing with the university; the judge’s decision leaves the phaseout dispute open rather than deciding whether the phones must ultimately remain.

In an affidavit described by Hearst, Contreras argues that a student’s personal phone may be unavailable, uncharged, lost, stolen or unusable during an emergency. His filing says removing a nearby fixed device without an equivalent replacement could create a gap in access to help. That is an allegation and safety argument from the plaintiff, not a court finding. The Oct. 9 proceeding is expected to give the parties a chance to discuss whether they can resolve the issue; if they cannot, the court may schedule a later evidentiary hearing.

UConn has defended the phaseout as a technology and cost decision. NBC Connecticut reported that the university says it received only two legitimate blue-phone calls in the past five years: one reporting a car crash and another from someone who believed they were being followed, a concern the university said was unfounded. The school told NBC that modernizing the system would cost about $6 million and that annual operating expenses exceed $70,000 as aging equipment requires more repairs.

The university is not planning to remove every phone. UConn has said it will keep devices in locations where cellular coverage is weaker and is assessing which sites meet that test. For other students, the school points to personal cellphone calls, text-to-911 and the LiveSafe app, which can connect users to the university’s Emergency Communications Center by text, video or phone. Students interviewed by NBC said those tools do not entirely replace a clearly marked device that can be activated without finding or unlocking a personal phone.

UConn’s own [Division of University Safety page](https://police.universitysafety.uconn.edu/emergency-blue-phones/) describes the existing Storrs system as a network of phones located throughout campus: a user presses a button, describes the emergency to a dispatcher and a police officer is sent to the location. That design matters to the dispute because the devices serve students, employees and visitors who may not have a working phone immediately available. The university’s current public description explains how the system operates, but it does not establish how many Storrs phones will remain after the review.

The question of usage is still developing. A Sept. 28 entry in [UConn’s public-records log](https://publicrecords.uconn.edu/requests/fpo-26-639-09-28-26-819-am/) shows an open request seeking the number of emergency blue phones at Storrs as of Aug. 31, the largest number ever installed and a year-by-year count of calls over the prior 25 calendar years. Those records could add context to the university’s five-year figures, but the request itself is not a response from the school and does not yet provide the requested data.

The next legal milestone is the Oct. 9 remote hearing. Until then, the court has not ordered UConn to stop its work, and the university’s plan to retain some phones in weak-service areas remains the stated approach. The case will turn on evidence about the remaining devices, their reliability and use, the alternatives available at each location and the practical safety consequences of removing them. For the Storrs community, the immediate issue is not whether cellphones are widespread; it is whether that coverage is sufficient at every place and moment where a person may need help.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: UConn parent asks court to halt blue-light phone removals
seoDescription: A UConn parent’s request to keep Storrs blue-light emergency phones operating will be heard Oct. 9 after a judge denied immediate relief.
